title: Test first, then fix
summary: Write a failing test that shows the bug, then fix the code until it passes.

say.never: When you find a bug, don't fix it yet. First write a test that shows it: the test should **FAIL** (red). Then fix the code until the test **PASSES** (green). Now the bug can never sneak back in, because that test would catch it. Pros call this **test-driven development**.
say.bit: Write a failing test for the bug first (red), then fix the code (green).

say.never: If you fix first, you never saw a test fail, so you don't know your test can catch the bug at all. Seeing red first proves the test works. Then seeing green proves the fix works.
say.bit: Red proves the test can catch the bug; green proves the fix works.

board.code:
FAIL earlyIsNotLate: expected false but was true
...fix the code...
PASS earlyIsNotLate

steps.title: In your lesson: Red, then green

say.never: `ShooterMath.isAtSpeed` says whether the flywheel is close enough to the target speed to shoot. Read it carefully. It's right when the wheel is a bit too fast, but what about when it's still spinning up and way too **slow**? Write tests for both sides, run them and watch one FAIL. Then fix `ShooterMath.java`.
say.bit: Test isAtSpeed on both sides of the target, watch one FAIL, then fix ShooterMath.
